long_description:
This Playbook aims to capture sustained upward trends across four major Bitget USDT perpetual markets while stepping aside when those trends fade. Its approach is built on a simple assumption: large crypto majors spend long stretches trending, and a patient trend filter on completed candles can stay invested through the middle of a rise without predicting every turning point. For each market independently, it compares a shorter moving-average view with a longer moving-average view of closed four-hour candles. When the shorter view is above the longer one, it holds a long position; when it is below, it holds no position in that market. It never opens short positions.

Position size follows a volatility target. Each market's weight starts from the configured target exposure and is scaled down when that market's recent realized volatility is high relative to the target, and never scaled up. When several markets are long at once, the aggregate gross cap of one times the margin budget is shared between them, so portfolio leverage never exceeds one. Positions are resized at each four-hour decision as prices and volatility change.

There is no independent take-profit or stop-loss. A long position is held while the trend relationship holds and is closed when the shorter view falls back below the longer one. Exits are late by design: moving averages lag, so a position can give back a meaningful part of a move before it closes, and sideways markets produce repeated entries and exits whose fees accumulate.

Because the strategy is long or flat, it depends on crypto majors rising over the long run. It does not profit from falling markets, and it pays funding while long, which becomes costly in heated bull markets. The four markets are highly correlated, so the volatility target reduces size without adding much diversification. Historical results were sensitive to the choice of moving-average lengths, and faster settings performed noticeably worse. Gaps, slippage, liquidation mechanics and fee differences can make live results diverge from historical evidence. Backtest returns are not forecasts; evaluate the displayed drawdown and execution evidence before subscribing.
